blocks.body:
## Technical summary

**KILL the dense/sparse router RTL.** Across 36.48M frozen 96-bit FC2 tiles, dense sequential is strictly faster than the exact K8 sparse issue floor on **zero** tiles at equal eight-bank bandwidth. Only 1,922 tiles (0.0053%) reach 50% density, and the best admitted router behavior is the no-op K8 baseline at 1.000×—below the predeclared 1.10× gate.

## The workload has no useful dense population

The chart partitions every tile into mutually exclusive nnz ranges. Nearly half are empty and another 49.0% contain only 1–23 events; just 0.0053% reach 48 events. A second dense path cannot be balanced or amortized from this tail.

## Tile stratification loses the bank aggregation that K8 already exploits

The sealed M216 full-vector K8 frontend takes 90.197M cycles. Its independently reproduced issue floor is 70.657M; closing sparse scheduling at every tile raises that zero-tax floor to 118.651M. This is already 1.315× slower before router, format, queue, or mode-switch tax.

## Scope and metric definitions

The population is Motion/H67 ep35 on `zurich_city_09_a`: ten frozen samples, twelve FC2 modules, 120 SHA-checked payloads, 5.58M tokens, and 143.895M nonzero events. One tile is a channel-contiguous 96-bit FC2 input slice for one token. Dense and sparse share eight logical weight banks with at most one source per bank per cycle.

## Methodology and robustness checks

The analyzer streams the sealed 350 MiB M51 tar.zst without extracting it, checks every selected member's size and SHA256, decodes little-endian channel bits, and independently conserves events at record, tile, bank, stage, and sample grain. All ten samples stay within 4.051%–4.153% event density; the result is not one-sample skew. A deliberately favorable control-overhead sensitivity routes only six tiles and yields at most 1.000000069× before any router tax.

## What transfers from Bishop and FireFly-T

[Bishop](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.12281) motivates heterogeneous routing only when dense and sparse work genuinely coexist and can balance dedicated cores. [FireFly-T](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.12771) motivates multi-nonzero decoding and bank-aware load balancing—support for closing the existing K8 path, not for adding a dense bypass. Neither paper's published performance is transferred to H67.

## Limitations and claim boundary

This is a trace-only CPU fast-kill for one DSEC sequence. It does not measure SRAM latency, accumulator/BN/residual commit, complete FC2 or FFN cycles, RTL, VCS, DC, SAIF/PTPX, energy, or full-network speedup. The energy sign remains unadmitted; dense mode necessarily fetches zero-source weight rows and also adds density detection, metadata, and merge logic.

## Recommended next steps

1. Do not create M517 router RTL or consume VCS/DC capacity.
2. Continue physical, equivalence, and energy closure of the shared-state K8 FC2 path.
3. Use M517 as a negative DSE result explaining why Bishop-style heterogeneity is workload-dependent.
4. Reopen only if a new checkpoint materially changes structured tile density; a new checkpoint requires a full identity-bound rerun.

## Further question

The only decision-relevant reopen condition is whether a future PAFT or rank-aware checkpoint creates a substantial, repeatable high-density FC2 population. Until then, the 1.10× gate remains failed.
